newsitem.title: CONGO: Ceasefire appears to be holding in Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Ceasefire appears to be holding in Brazzaville.

text.p: Fighting died down in Congo's capital Brazzaville on Thursday as a ceasefire appeared to be holding after a week of fierce clashes between forces loyal to the president and a former Marxist military ruler.
Only occasional shots could be heard in the city centre wrecked by the fighting between President Pascal Lissouba's troops and the Cobra militia of Denis Sassou Nguesso before Wednesday's ceasefire.
French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, escorted by armoured personnel carriers on a tour of looted French property in the city, told reporters when asked if the ceasefire was holding:
"I think so and I hope so...I think the worst is over."
As he went into some of the looted buildings, shots rang out from nearby areas while the sound of rocket-propelled grenade explosions could be heard from far away.
Earlier on Thursday mortar blasts and grenade explosions echoed around some areas near the Brazzaville airport after sporadic shooting overnight.
French military spokesman Captain Alexis Jaraud told Reuters: "It's much more calm today than it has been before. Really there is nothing happening."
Clashes had erupted last week after government troops surrounded the home of Sassou Nguesso in a crackdown on militias ahead of a July 27 presidential election.
In the city centre, the body of a boy of about eight lay on the roadside in an area controlled by Sassou Nguesso's forces -- with a gunshot in the head and his school bag still on his back.
Corpses lay in other streets, but no overall death toll was available because aid worker and military officials had not reached all areas of fighting.
Many shops were looted and several buildings were burned down.
France, Congo's former colonial ruler, said on Wednesday its armed forces had evacuated 1,778 foreigners, two-thirds of them French nationals, to nearby Gabon by air since Monday.

"What is important is that the chain of command should be re-established, because the men on the ground are left to themselves for the moment. I would like it if they would withdraw to districts where they can receive orders," Cesaire said.
"We have a very special relationship (with Congo) and we cannot abandon it. For us it is very important to re-establish calm," he said.

But the ambassador declined to comment when asked whether he had said, as reported by Brazzaville Mayor Bernard Kolelas on Wednesday, that France was ready to put a buffer force between the two sides.
On Wednesday, Lissouba ordered an unilateral ceasefire to allow for mediation. Hours later, Sassou Nguesso ordered his forces to stop firing.

Lissouba's ceasefire call followed a meeting on Tuesday with Kolelas, who is chairing a mediation committee of the two sides. A spokesman for Kolelas said that he had spoken by telephone on Wednesday with Sassou Nguesso.

Lissouba won a 1992 presidential election after Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979, bowed to calls for multi-party politics. Lissouba defeated Kolelas in the second round after Sassou Nguesso was knocked out in the first round.
Kolelas's Ninja militia was at the heart of similar fighting which killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 and early 1994, but it has kept out of the latest fighting.
